historical_prior_reviews.inspection_scope: All machine-readable text indexed; targeted contents/context inspection only unless separately stated. Figure geometry unmeasured.; inspected viewer pages [1, 2, 3]
historical_prior_reviews.what_changes: Keep the Second Temple chronology unknown. LIMIT: Report text fully read.

new_evidence.observation: The report dates abandonment of the main estate to 144–143 BCE and records a later short-lived 7×7 m tower built over the summit structure.
new_evidence.interpretation: The tower is plausibly late second century BCE and may reflect Hasmonean control.
new_evidence.project_inference: A claim of no later settlement must retain the later tower exception; estate and tower are separate phases.

new_evidence.observation: Body assigns dipinti to figure15/16/17; final caption list and plate12 assign same images13/14/15.
new_evidence.project_inference: Use actual plate/caption numbering when archiving, document mismatch instead of silently changing source references.

new_evidence.observation: Figure2 labels Pit A bottom182.153 m asl and Pit B182.632 m asl; its caption says the leveled floor is schematic. The embedded coin table prints Herod40 CE and Agrippa II41/2 CE; these literal source labels are retained.
new_evidence.project_inference: Do not treat schematic section as precise ancient floor geometry or silently repair coin-table labels.
new_evidence.interpretation: The report dates the lowest fill Early Roman and upper fill Late Roman, disturbed after abandonment.

new_evidence.observation: The9×9 m summit building incorporates an earlier storage shaft. The elongated cistern floor remains beneath unexcavated sediment.
new_evidence.interpretation: The standing building could be Late Roman/Early Byzantine or medieval if the proposed groin vault is confirmed; the authors call for excavation. The cistern is assigned to the Second Temple period from plaster and morphology.
new_evidence.project_inference: The interpretation of the site as a Hasmonean fortress does not date the standing summit building or its floor.

new_evidence.observation: Possible threshold L265 lies below W166 and connects to entrance G,0.71×0.52 m. The earliest phases VI–V lack secure dates. Coin appendix No.1 is a67/68 CE First Revolt coin in L119/B1274; Mamluk coin No.12 is also from L119, basket1049.
new_evidence.interpretation: The earliest rock-cut and building phases may both be Byzantine; the report explicitly leaves their date unknown.
new_evidence.project_inference: An early coin without a sealed construction context cannot establish a First Century date for the threshold.

new_evidence.observation: Removing a bulging modern foundation exposed a4.2 m gap within the gate wall. Fields C/D excavated in2015 show the ditch cutting earlier structures.
new_evidence.interpretation: The authors reconstruct the gateway by comparison; ditch width and depth of roughly15 m are estimates and the original gate construction remains undated.
new_evidence.project_inference: A negative excavation result tests the accessed ancient volume; an earlier investigation with limited visibility can miss a feature later exposed.

new_evidence.observation: C2 has seven descending steps, a collecting vat, a channel ending at a trapezoidal basin, and Late Roman ribbed pottery embedded in plaster. C1 shaft L305 and area D pit were not excavated because of collapse risk.
new_evidence.interpretation: Authors identify C2 as a winepress; embedded pottery dates its plaster to the Late Roman period.
new_evidence.project_inference: Do not classify this stepped vat as a Second Temple ritual bath; unexcavated shafts retain unknown geometry and dates.

new_evidence.observation: Quantitative charts account for 123 identifiable glass vessels; chamber count charts total 123. The hall G/H/Z subset totals 81.
new_evidence.interpretation: Typology supports glass dated between 70 and 135/136 CE. Authors propose sudden abandonment but say this inference is inconclusive.
new_evidence.project_inference: Vessel counts cannot establish numbers of occupants. The glass article and cave coin chronology share the same 2009 campaign and must not be counted as fully independent discoveries.

new_evidence.observation: Footnote 29 attributes all architectural descriptions to Magen 1990/2012. Figures 4, 6 and 7 reproduce Magen; Figure 5 is from Biblewalks. Early coins include a coin of 31 CE without a reported sealed building context.
new_evidence.interpretation: The author assigns fort construction to the late fourth or early fifth century.
new_evidence.project_inference: This article is a derivative architectural synthesis, not a new field record establishing a First Century construction date.

new_evidence.observation: Authors restrict field work to surface visits and road-linked sites; they explicitly warn that absent period pottery cannot establish absence of occupation. Lydda–Emmaus has no preserved Roman road remains and its alignment is theoretical. The Burej road cross-sections are measured, but the only chronological evidence is Late Roman/Byzantine surface pottery.
new_evidence.interpretation: Milestones support reconstructing the Emmaus–Beit Horon road more securely than the theoretical Lydda–Emmaus line.
new_evidence.project_inference: Keep survey absence, predicted road alignment, measured road geometry and construction dating as separate evidence classes.

new_evidence.observation: At Daliya the surface survey attributed 86% of collected pottery to the Byzantine period, while the later limited excavation found the bulk of pottery and coins to be Early Roman. Gibeon excavation target focused on the Biblical hill while later remains lay mostly beneath the modern village. Kafr Rut surface report contains no Second Temple or Roman material, yet its subterranean systems are discussed separately in the appendix.
new_evidence.interpretation: Authors call Daliya a clear example of misleading surface-only chronology and discuss investigation bias at Gibeon.
new_evidence.project_inference: A surface assemblage, a sampled excavation area and a subterranean feature need separate coverage statements; no-period sherd absence is not a site-wide negative test.

new_evidence.observation: Mazad has several architectural phases. The3.5 m square,2.24 m deep stepped cistern is explicitly a possible ritual bath requiring investigation. A162 CE milestone is reused in the Byzantine structure. The Ha-Gardi description derives from earlier surveys and distinguishes several tomb phases.
new_evidence.interpretation: Mazad began with a Hasmonean tower, expanded in the Herodian period, and was rebuilt in Byzantine/Early Islamic phases. The Ha-Gardi cross mosaic belongs to a fifth-century or later Christian phase.
new_evidence.project_inference: Reused inscriptions and late phases cannot supply construction dates for the original cistern, threshold or tomb.

new_evidence.observation: The pottery appendix cites figures24–33 while the corresponding actual plates are captioned Figures20–29, an offset of four. It publishes pottery for only20 of133 sites; most are surface finds.
new_evidence.interpretation: The authors use excavated sites as chronological models and explicitly limit the survey assemblages to a small part of site history.
new_evidence.project_inference: Archive the actual caption numbers and retain the citation mismatch. Unpublished or absent surface pottery is not proof of no occupation.

new_evidence.observation: Er-Ras caves were reconstructed from surviving plaster and blocked passages. Three coins were found in piles of earth. Narrative calls one Bar Kokhba coin undated, while the catalogue assigns it to year2. Kureikur has no dating sherds in the surveyed complex.
new_evidence.interpretation: The appendix authors relate the complexes to Bar Kokhba; Isaac’s introduction records disagreement over whether every hideout is exclusive to that revolt.
new_evidence.project_inference: Separate measured morphology, reconstructed inaccessible branches, loose coin associations and historical attribution; do not silently resolve the coin-date disagreement.

new_evidence.observation: Site totals combine farmsteads and cities; a watchtower and legionary base are equally counted. Surface coverage cannot measure settlement extent, and archaeological artifacts do not establish ethnic affiliation. Pre-Roman roads are inferred from later routes and occupied sites.
new_evidence.interpretation: The authors identify broad settlement shifts and road/site coexistence but cannot determine whether roads caused settlement growth or settlement caused road construction.
new_evidence.project_inference: These tables/maps are regional controls with survey limits, not complete demographic counts, causal tests, or site-wide negatives.
